props.title: Death Proof
props.initialSlug: Buckle up for the ride of death.

sections.content: Death Proof represents Quentin Tarantino's visceral love letter to muscle car exploitation films and slasher flicks. Kurt Russell delivers a menacing performance as Stuntman Mike, a scarred killer who weaponizes his "death proof" stunt car against unsuspecting women. The film's brilliant structural shift - from stalker horror to revenge thriller - culminates in one of cinema's greatest car chases, with real stunt work by Zoë Bell (playing herself) on the hood of a 1970 Dodge Challenger. Shot on grainy film stock with deliberate scratches and missing reels, it perfectly captures the gritty aesthetic of 1970s grindhouse cinema.

sections.content: The DNA of Death Proof flows directly from the golden age of car chase cinema. Bullitt (1968) set the template with its San Francisco pursuit, while The French Connection (1971) brought documentary-style intensity to urban car action. These influences crystallized in Mad Max (1979), where vehicles become both weapons and characters themselves - a concept Tarantino explicitly borrows for Stuntman Mike's murderous muscle car. SUBHEAD: The Grindhouse Revival Connection

As one half of the Grindhouse (2007) double feature with Robert Rodriguez's Planet Terror (2007), Death Proof deliberately channels exploitation classics like I Spit on Your Grave (1978) and Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill! (1965). The film's feminist revenge finale, with stuntwoman Kim (Tracie Thoms) and driver Zoë turning the tables on their stalker, directly inverts slasher film tropes established in Halloween (1978) and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974).
